title: What is Investment Banking?
body: Investment banks help companies and governments raise money and provide advice on major financial transactions like mergers, acquisitions, and IPOs.
callout: Think of an investment bank as a financial advisor for big companies — not for individuals.

left.heading: Buy-Side
left.body: The bank advises a company that wants to BUY another company.
left.example: Example: Disney buying Pixar — an investment bank helped Disney decide the right price and structure.
left.quote: "SpaceX was the Buy-Side on their acquisition of XAI"

right.heading: Sell-Side
right.body: The bank advises a company that is being SOLD or is looking for a buyer.
right.example: Example: LinkedIn selling to Microsoft — LinkedIn's bank helped find the best deal.
right.quote: "XAI was on the Sell-Side of the transaction"

title: M&A Scenario — Answers
buy_side: MICROSOFT acquires Activision — Microsoft is the buyer
DISNEY buys Pixar — Disney is the acquirer
sell_side: LINKEDIN sells to Microsoft — LinkedIn's bank finds the best deal
WARNER BROS. sells its music division — WB is the seller
key_insight: The same company can be on different sides in different deals. Ask: are they gaining or giving up ownership? Gaining → Buy-Side. Giving up → Sell-Side.

title: Function 2: Capital Markets (IPO)
instruction: Click each step card to learn what happens at that stage.
subtitle: Tap any card below to reveal details about that stage of the IPO.

title: IPO Step 1: Company Needs $$$
body: A private company decides it needs to raise a large amount of money.

rows.desc: Expand into new markets, hire, build products
Replace expensive debt with equity capital

key_point: The company hires an investment bank to manage the IPO process.

title: IPO Step 2: Bank Sets the Price
body: The investment bank (underwriter) determines how much each share should cost.

rows.desc: DCF, comparable companies, and precedent transactions to estimate the company's worth
Company and bankers tour institutional investors to pitch the stock and gauge demand
Collect buy orders from investors to determine the final price range

key_point: The final IPO price balances company valuation with investor demand.

title: IPO Step 3: Bank Sells Shares
body: On pricing night, the bank commits to buying all the shares from the company at the IPO price. Then it sells (allocates) them to investors. This is called underwriting.

flow.label: Company
flow.sub: Sells shares to bank at IPO price

callout: The bank takes on risk — if they can't sell the shares, they're stuck holding them. That's why the bank earns a fee (the "spread") of ~3–7% of total proceeds.

title: IPO Step 4: Company Is Now Public
body: On the first trading day, the company's shares begin trading on a stock exchange (NYSE or NASDAQ). Anyone can now buy and sell the stock.

rows.desc: Must file 10-K, 10-Q, and disclose financials to the SEC
Stock price now determines the company's market cap in real time
Founders, employees, and VCs can eventually sell their shares

key_point: The IPO is complete. The bank's job is done (except for a stabilization period).

title: Key Takeaways
points: IB helps companies with major financial transactions — not personal banking
Advisory (M&A): Advising on buying or selling companies (Buy-Side vs. Sell-Side)
Capital Markets: Helping companies raise money through IPOs
IPO process: Company needs $$$ → Bank prices → Bank sells → Company goes public
Deal flow: Pitch → Due Diligence → Negotiation → Execution
